predictions.title: Second hyperscaler names non-Nvidia data-center inference silicon by Q4 2027
predictions.body: Qualcomm's June 24 Dragonfly data-center roadmap did something its prior server-silicon pushes never managed: it attached a named hyperscaler, with Meta committing to the Dragonfly C1000 CPU for its next-generation server fleet at the part's 2028 commercial availability, alongside a Dragonfly AI300 inference accelerator and a High Bandwidth Compute memory tier pitched explicitly at Nvidia's inference economics. The named-customer reference, not the silicon specs, is the competitive trigger: once one hyperscaler is on the record backing a merchant non-Nvidia inference stack, the inference-economics argument moves from vendor marketing to a peer-validated procurement signal that rival cloud operators must answer. The prediction is that a second top-tier hyperscaler (among Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle, Meta, or a comparable named operator distinct from Meta) will publicly commit to a named non-Nvidia data-center CPU or inference-accelerator partner — whether Qualcomm, AMD, a merchant rival, or its own custom-silicon arm announced as a named external design win — within a concrete window. The forcing function is that inference cost-per-token is now the dominant data-center economic line as agentic workloads scale, and no hyperscaler can let a competitor lock in a cheaper inference floor unanswered.

reasoning.because: Qualcomm's June 24 Dragonfly roadmap put Meta on record as its first named data-center CPU customer
reasoning.given: inference cost-per-token is now the dominant data-center economic line as agentic workloads scale
reasoning.so_that: a second hyperscaler publicly commits to a named non-Nvidia data-center CPU or inference-accelerator partner
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2027; one second named hyperscaler-plus-vendor inference-silicon commitment
reasoning.plain_language: After Meta backed a non-Nvidia AI server chip, another big cloud company will publicly pick one too.

predictions.summary: Qualcomm's Dragonfly roadmap named Meta as its first data-center CPU customer, turning the inference-economics attack on Nvidia into a peer-validated procurement signal. With inference cost-per-token now the dominant cloud economic line, expect a second top-tier hyperscaler to publicly commit to a named non-Nvidia data-center CPU or inference-accelerator partner by Q4 2027.

predictions.title: HBM allocation becomes a named binding cap in a vendor disclosure by Q2 2027
predictions.body: Micron's fiscal-Q3-2026 print reframes the AI buildout as a memory-supply story: revenue of $41.46 billion (up ~346% year over year), HBM sold out across all of 2026, a CEO admission that Micron can fill only half to two-thirds of HBM demand, HBM4 revenue past $1 billion and ramping about twice as fast as HBM3E, and 16 take-or-pay Strategic Customer Agreements locking in roughly $100 billion of minimum contracted revenue plus $22 billion of upfront customer cash. With supply pre-committed years out and demand structurally short, high-bandwidth memory — not just GPUs — is now the binding constraint on how many accelerators can actually ship. The prediction is that at least one major accelerator vendor or hyperscaler will, in an earnings call, guidance document, or capacity-roadmap disclosure, explicitly name HBM allocation or take-or-pay memory contracting as a gating limit on its accelerator shipments or AI-capacity ramp, rather than treating memory as a fungible component. The forcing function is competitive scarcity: when one buyer locks multi-year take-or-pay memory supply, rivals must either secure comparable contracts or publicly concede a capacity ceiling, and the first to disclose the constraint sets the narrative.

reasoning.because: Micron reported HBM sold out through 2026, fillable only to half-to-two-thirds of demand, under ~$100B take-or-pay
reasoning.given: memory supply is pre-committed years out, making HBM allocation the binding cap on accelerator shipments
reasoning.so_that: an accelerator vendor or hyperscaler names HBM allocation as a stated gating limit on its shipment or capacity ramp
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; >=1 vendor or hyperscaler names HBM as a binding cap
reasoning.plain_language: Memory chips for AI are so sold out that a big chip or cloud company will admit they limit how much AI it can build.

predictions.summary: Micron reported HBM sold out through 2026, fillable to only half-to-two-thirds of demand, with ~$100B of take-or-pay customer contracts and $22B upfront cash. That makes high-bandwidth memory, not just GPUs, the binding cap on accelerator output. Expect at least one accelerator vendor or hyperscaler to name HBM allocation as a stated gating limit on shipments or AI-capacity by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Sovereign-AI national champion crosses unicorn valuation by Q4 2026
predictions.body: Sarvam's jump to a $1.5 billion valuation on HCLTech's $234 million first close — a strategic IT-services check, not a pure venture round, taking a ~10.5% stake to fund a frontier coding/agentic/cybersecurity model built and governed inside India — is the template for how sovereign-AI money is now mobilized. Gartner's forecast that agent software alone reaches about $206.5 billion in 2026, growing nearly triple the 47% pace of overall AI spend, gives national governments and their domestic IT/telecom incumbents the demand signal to bankroll an in-country model builder rather than route the workload to US frontier labs. The prediction is that at least one additional sovereign-AI model builder outside the US and China — in a market such as the Gulf, Southeast Asia, the EU, Japan, or Korea — crosses the $1 billion valuation threshold via a round anchored by a domestic strategic (a national telecom, IT-services firm, or sovereign-wealth/state vehicle) rather than a Western VC. The forcing function is that data-residency and governance mandates make a domestically hosted, locally controlled model a procurement requirement, and the cheapest way to guarantee that is to own equity in the builder.

reasoning.because: HCLTech's $234M strategic first close minted Sarvam at a $1.5B sovereign-AI unicorn valuation
reasoning.given: Gartner sees agent software at ~$206.5B in 2026, growing nearly 3x overall AI spend
reasoning.so_that: another non-US/China sovereign-AI model builder crosses $1B on a domestic-strategic-anchored round
reasoning.landing: A new sovereign-AI unicorn is minted on a strategic-led round by Q4 2026
reasoning.plain_language: Another country will fund its own homegrown AI company past a billion-dollar value, backed by a local big business.

predictions.summary: HCLTech's $234M strategic first close valued Sarvam at $1.5B, and Gartner sees agent software hitting ~$206.5B in 2026, pulling national champions into the capital flow. Expect at least one more sovereign-AI model builder outside the US and China to cross a $1B valuation on a domestic-strategic-anchored round by Q4 2026.
